The study aimed to investigate the correlations among immune, haematological, endocrinological markers and fitness parameters, and assess if the physiological parameters could be a predictor of fitness values. Anthropometric, physical evaluations (countermovement jump—CMJ, 10 m sprint, VO 2 max, repeated sprint ability—RSA total time and index) and determination of blood (IL-6, IL-10, IL-17A and tumour necrosis factor) and salivary (testosterone and cortisol) samples parameters in 28 young male soccer players (age: 13.0 ± 0.2 years, body mass index (BMI): 19.5 ± 2.2 kg/m 2 ) were analysed. To evaluate the dependence of the variables related to athletic performance, multiple linear regression with backward stepwise elimination was considered. A significant regression equation was found in CMJ (F (5,16) = 9.86, p < 0.001, R 2 adjusted = 0.679) and in the RSA index (F (5,16) = 15.39, p < 0.001, R 2 adjusted = 0.774) considering only five variables, in a 10 m sprint (F (4,17) = 20.25, p < 0.001, R 2 adjusted = 0.786) and in the RSA total time (F (4,17) = 15.31, p < 0.001, R 2 adjusted = 0.732) considering only four variables and in VO 2 max (F (9,12) = 32.09, p < 0.001, R 2 adjusted = 0.930) considering nine variables. Our study suggests the use of regression equations to predict the fitness values of youth soccer players by blood and saliva samples, during different phases of the season, short periods of match congestion or recovery from an injury. cortisol countermovement jump cytokines maximal oxygen uptake 1. Introduction Several studies have reported that repeated physical and psychological stressors lead to haematological, inflammatory and endocrine changes, which result in adaptive physiological responses and affect the physical performance of sports players [ 1 , 2 ]. Furthermore, growing evidence supports the hypothesis that, during the young soccer player agonistic season, correct maintenance of homeostasis is finely regulated through the immune, haematological and endocrine systems interaction, and contributes to the athlete performance and physical integrity [ 3 , 4 ]. Therefore, several biochemical markers could be used as indicators for physical stress, systemic inflammation, muscle damage and physiological adaptation to sports activity [ 5 , 6 , 7 ]. In this regard, testosterone (T) and cortisol (C) play an important role in exercise-related stress. T is mainly involved in anabolic processes, which support healthy muscle development [ 8 ], while C is a strong indicator of catabolic metabolism [ 9 ]. The T/C ratio has been positively related to changes in physical performance and indicated as a balance of anabolic/catabolic activity [ 10 ], representing a useful tool in the early detection of overtraining [ 11 ]. Our group [ 12 ] found significant correlations between fitness and hormonal parameters in youth soccer players before the beginning of 8-weeks of the preseason training phase. Other authors [ 13 , 14 ] showed significant alterations in the hormonal concentrations in the young soccer players during the six-month of the competitive season. Despite its diffusion and popularity, very few studies have been carried out on evaluating biochemical, haematological and endocrine parameters metabolism of youth soccer players. Concerning the exercise-induced inflammation, the role of some cytokines, proteins with several pleiotropic effects involved in cell signalling during inflammatory responses [ 15 ], should be better elucidated. Araujo et al. [ 16 ] suggested that physical training induces adaptations to the stress mediated by an immune response, resulting by changes in the cytokine profile. However, pro-inflammatory cytokines (including IL-6, TNF-alpha and IL-17AA) may be preferentially upregulated during acute exercise, while chronically prolonged physical activity may promote an anti-inflammatory status presumably associated with IL-10 secretion [ 3 , 4 , 14 , 17 , 18 , 19 ]. Furthermore, Heisterberg et al. [ 20 ] have shown that variations of haemoglobin and haematocrit were related to the amount of aerobic and anaerobic training, strength training and the number of matches per week in professional soccer players. Silva et al. [ 21 ] showed that soccer players face significant changes in biomarkers of physiologic strain (muscle damage and oxidative stress-related markers) during the competitive season, but values return to normal during the off-season. The aim of the present study was to investigate if some biological parameters could be predictive of fitness values in youth soccer players, throughout the whole season. The majority of reports in this field were previously focused on measures of performance, progress in training and identifying overtraining [ 22 ]. To our knowledge, this is the first attempt to predict fitness values in order to provide trainers and sports physicians useful reports on performance and physiological adaptations of their soccer players in specific moments of a season (i.e., short periods of match congestion).

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Repeated physical and psychological stressors, including strenuous pre-seasonal training loads and the agonistic season, in youth soccer players.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Repeated physical and psychological stressors, including exercise-induced muscle stress and training loads, lead to haematological, inflammatory, and endocrine changes that affect physical performance. During the agonistic season, homeostasis is regulated by the immune, haematological, and endocrine systems. Testosterone primarily supports anabolic muscle development, while cortisol indicates catabolic metabolism; their ratio (T/C) balances these activities and can signal overtraining. Acute exercise may upregulate pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-"alpha", IL-17A), whereas chronic physical activity can promote an anti-inflammatory state associated with IL-10 secretion. Biomarkers like IL-6 and cortisol are stress-induced, while IL-10 and haematocrit may reflect adaptive responses to training. Monitoring these biomarkers helps assess physiological homeostasis; an imbalance, particularly between pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines, can indicate overtraining.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: The study observed physiological changes attributed to a brief but strenuous pre-seasonal training load. It notes that pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-alpha, IL-17A) are upregulated during acute exercise, while chronic activity promotes an anti-inflammatory status linked to IL-10 secretion. Variations in haemoglobin and haematocrit correlate with the amount of aerobic/anaerobic training, strength training, and match frequency. The T/C ratio is highlighted for early detection of overtraining, indicating adaptive biomarker responses to increasing training loads.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding:
The study specifically focused on predicting fitness values in youth male soccer players (aged 13.0 

0.2 years) across different seasonal phases, match congestion, or injury recovery periods, marking it as a novel attempt in this specific context. Significant regression equations were developed for various fitness parameters (CMJ, 10m sprint, VO2 max, RSA Total Time, RSA Index), indicating specific predictive relationships between distinct panels of biochemical markers and individual physical performance outcomes.

clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: The study provides a predictive tool using physiological parameters for youth soccer players' fitness values, enabling trainers and sports physicians to systematically monitor athlete performance, physiological adaptations, and overload throughout the competitive season. This can optimize efficiency, prevent overtraining and injuries, assess physical attitude, and contribute to talent identification, performance monitoring, and maintaining athlete physical integrity and homeostasis.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: The biomarkers offer diagnostic utility as predictive indices for fitness values and early detection of overtraining in youth soccer players. They provide a protective benefit by enabling monitoring to prevent overtraining and injuries, thereby optimizing performance and maintaining physiological homeostasis. An adverse risk is associated with imbalanced pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines, which can lead to overtraining and increased injury risk.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The study's multifactorial linear regression models demonstrated significant predictive power (p < 0.001) with high adjusted R^2 values (0.679 to 0.930) for various fitness parameters (CMJ, RSA index, 10m sprint, RSA total time, VO2max) using immune, haematological, and endocrinological markers, suggesting reliability for these predictive models. While previous attempts with biochemical markers faced interindividual variability and debated correlations, the study's approach appears robust. Additionally, the 10m sprint and Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 1 (YYIRT1) were confirmed as valid and reliable, and salivary testosterone and cortisol assays exhibited high sensitivity and low inter-/intra-assay coefficients of variation (<10% and 5% respectively).
recommended_alternatives: The study emphasizes a 'multifactorial approach' utilizing a comprehensive panel of performance tests (CMJ, 10m sprint, VO2 max, RSA) combined with common blood-based inflammatory and endocrinological biomarkers (IL-6, IL-10, IL-17, TNF-"alpha", Cortisol, Testosterone, erythrocyte, haematocrit, thrombocyte, PCR, leucocyte) for athlete monitoring.
Future studies are recommended to validate this multifactorial approach in broader populations, including youth of different ages, adult, and female soccer players.
The implementation of additional blood biomarkers as monitoring tools is suggested for deeper insights into athlete health, performance, and recovery.
